The story makes sophisticated use of metaphor (as well as closely related figurative comparisons like similes and personification) to deepen the emotional resonance and develop the characters. 

For example, the narrator describes Toby as a man who had decided "that the ocean was not scenery but a colleague," which immediately establishes his pragmatic, professional, and slightly guarded approach to the world. Later, when Toby removes the borrowed wetsuit, the narrator refers to it as "the costume," metaphorically linking the physical gear to the emotional armor and temporary roles both characters have been wearing throughout their six-week residency. 

Furthermore, the central predicament of the story—getting stranded on the mud flats by the rising tide—serves as an extended metaphor for their relationship. Having spent the entire summer avoiding the reality of their impending separation, they only confront their true feelings when they are "genuinely, physically, mutually stuck" and the ocean returns "like a debt collector," forcing them to finally reckon with what they owe to themselves and each other.
